**Yarra Valley** is a cool-climate wine region in Victoria, Australia, just north-east of Melbourne, and one of the country's most respected areas for elegant, restrained styles.

**Wines & grapes** — Pinot Noir and Chardonnay lead the way, both as still wines and as the base for high-quality traditional-method sparkling. Cool-grown Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon also do well.

**Character** — Its relatively cool, sometimes marginal climate means grapes ripen slowly, yielding wines with finesse, freshness and moderate alcohol rather than sheer power. The valley's mix of altitudes and aspects lets growers match varieties to sites with real precision.

**Good to know** — As one of Victoria's oldest wine areas, it was a pioneer of cool-climate winemaking in Australia.

name: Bekaa Valley
description:
**Bekaa Valley** is the beating heart of Lebanese wine, a high plateau set between mountain ranges in the east of the country.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds dominate, built around French varieties like Cinsault, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Grenache, often in blends; there are also whites from grapes such as the local Obeideh and Merwah as well as international varieties.

**Character** — Sitting at considerable altitude, the valley enjoys hot days and cool nights, plenty of sunshine and low disease pressure, conditions that ripen grapes fully while keeping good acidity. The wines are typically warm and full-bodied yet balanced.

**Good to know** — Lebanon has one of the world's oldest winemaking traditions, stretching back to the ancient Phoenicians.

name: Vinho Verde
description:
**Vinho Verde** comes from the Minho region in the cool, green, rainy north-west of Portugal, and the name means "green wine" in the sense of young and fresh rather than any colour.

**Wines & grapes** — It is best known for light, zesty whites, often with a faint natural spritz, made from grapes like Alvarinho, Loureiro, Trajadura and Arinto. Reds and rosés are also produced, though the crisp whites define the region.

**Character** — The damp Atlantic climate and lush landscape yield wines that are low in alcohol, high in acidity and delightfully refreshing. Traditionally the vines were trained high to cope with the humidity, and the top expressions — especially single-varietal Alvarinho — can show real depth and structure.

name: Kakheti
description:
**Kakheti** in eastern Georgia is the country's most important wine region, at the centre of a winemaking culture that reaches back thousands of years.

**Wines & grapes** — The dark-skinned Saperavi makes deep, robust reds, while Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane give the whites; many are made in the traditional amber (or "orange") style with extended skin contact.

**Character** — What sets Kakheti apart is the ancient *qvevri* method, in which grapes ferment and age in large clay vessels buried in the ground, giving whites a tannic grip and savoury, nutty character unlike almost anywhere else.

**Good to know** — Georgia is often described as one of the birthplaces of wine, and the qvevri tradition is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.

name: Eden Valley
description:
**Eden Valley** is a cooler, higher-altitude wine region in South Australia, tucked into the hills adjoining the Barossa, and is prized above all for its whites.

**Wines & grapes** — Riesling is the headline grape, producing dry, tightly focused whites with great ageing potential, while Shiraz here takes on a more elegant, spicy form than in the warmer valley floor below.

**Character** — The elevation brings cooler nights and a longer growing season, so the wines gain a fineness and lift you don't always find in the Barossa. Eden Valley Riesling is famous for its citrus and floral notes when young and its toasty, honeyed complexity with age.

**Good to know** — Some of Australia's oldest Riesling vineyards are found in these hills.

name: Tejo
description:
**Tejo** is a wine region in central Portugal named after the Tagus (Tejo) river, whose fertile plains and surrounding hills it straddles; it was formerly known as Ribatejo.

**Wines & grapes** — A wide range of styles is made from both native and international grapes, with reds built on Castelão, Touriga Nacional and Trincadeira, and whites from Fernão Pires and Arinto among others.

**Character** — The river shapes the region: the warmer, more fertile riverside land yields softer, approachable everyday wines, while the cooler, poorer soils away from the water give more structured, characterful bottles. Overall Tejo offers friendly, well-priced Portuguese wines with plenty of ripe, sunny fruit.

name: Minho
description:
**Minho** is a green, rainy province in the far northwest of Portugal, tucked between the Douro and the Spanish border, and it is the home of the country's most famous fresh white style, Vinho Verde.

**Wines & grapes** — This is the heartland of Vinho Verde, mostly crisp whites from grapes such as Alvarinho, Loureiro, Trajadura and Arinto, though light reds and rosés are made too. Bottlings range from simple, faintly fizzy quaffers to serious, mineral single-varietal Alvarinho.

**Character** — The Atlantic climate is cool and wet, so the wines tend to be low in alcohol, high in zippy acidity and often finished with a light spritz. Expect green-apple, citrus and floral notes and a clean, thirst-quenching bite.

**Good to know** — "Verde" means young and fresh here, not literally green in colour.

name: Vin de France
description:
**Vin de France** is not a place but France's most flexible national wine category, replacing the old "Vin de Table" tier and covering wine from anywhere in the country.

**Wines & grapes** — Any style and almost any grape is allowed, and unusually for France, producers may name the grape variety and vintage on the label. It spans everything from cheap everyday bottles to ambitious "declassified" wines made outside the strict appellation rules.

**Character** — Because it carries no geographic or stylistic constraints, quality varies enormously: some are simple blends, others are boundary-pushing cuvées from serious growers who want creative freedom.

**Good to know** — A Vin de France label tells you little on its own, so the producer's name is your best guide to what's inside.

name: Dalmatia
description:
**Dalmatia** is Croatia's long, sun-soaked Adriatic coastline and its islands, one of the country's most historic and distinctive wine zones.

**Wines & grapes** — The signature red is Plavac Mali, which gives dark, powerful wines, while whites lean on local grapes such as Pošip and Maraština. Plavac Mali is a descendant of Zinfandel, which is native to this coast, where it is known as Tribidrag or Crljenak Kaštelanski.

**Character** — Baking Mediterranean sun, steep stony slopes and sea breezes produce concentrated, high-alcohol reds with ripe dark fruit and herbal, saline edges, alongside fresh, characterful whites.

**Good to know** — Steep coastal sites like Dingač and Postup on the Pelješac peninsula are among Dalmatia's most prized vineyards.

name: Navarra
description:
**Navarra** is a wine region in northern Spain, just east of Rioja, historically famous for rosé but today making a wide spread of styles.

**Wines & grapes** — Garnacha (Grenache) is the traditional backbone, long used for vivid, fruity rosados, while reds and blends also feature Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Whites and sweet Moscatel are made as well.

**Character** — The region bridges Atlantic, continental and Mediterranean influences, giving cooler, fresher wines in the north and riper, fuller ones in the warmer south. Overall the reds are approachable and fruit-forward, and the rosés bright and dry.

**Good to know** — Navarra earned its early reputation on Garnacha rosé before international grapes broadened its range.

name: Castilla
description:
**Castilla** is a broad wine designation covering the vast central Spanish plateau of Castilla-La Mancha, south of Madrid.

**Wines & grapes** — As a regional (Vino de la Tierra) category it allows a huge palette of grapes, from the white workhorse Airén to reds like Tempranillo (locally Cencibel), Garnacha and international varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.

**Character** — This is high, dry, sun-drenched country with hot days and cold nights, producing generous, ripe, mostly affordable wines. The looser regional rules give growers freedom to blend and experiment beyond the stricter local appellations.

**Good to know** — The wider Castilla-La Mancha area is one of the largest continuous vineyard expanses on earth.

name: Virginia
description:
**Virginia** is a wine state on the mid-Atlantic coast of the United States, with a long history dating back to early colonial attempts at winegrowing.

**Wines & grapes** — Its calling-card grape is Viognier, giving perfumed, peachy whites, while reds often come from Bordeaux varieties and the hybrid Norton. Petit Verdot and Cabernet Franc do particularly well.

**Character** — A humid, sometimes stormy continental climate makes viticulture challenging, but the wines tend toward a fresher, more restrained, European-leaning style than warmer US regions. Elegance and moderate alcohol are common threads.

**Good to know** — Virginia has embraced Viognier almost as an unofficial signature grape.

name: Ohio
description:
**Ohio** is a wine-producing state in the American Midwest, with vineyards concentrated near Lake Erie and along the Ohio River valley.

**Wines & grapes** — Cool-climate and hybrid grapes feature strongly, including Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc and native or hybrid varieties like Catawba and Concord. Both dry table wines and sweeter styles are made.

**Character** — The moderating effect of Lake Erie helps temper harsh winters, and the wines are generally fresh and light-to-medium bodied. Local grape varieties give some bottlings a distinctive, foxy or grapey character.

**Good to know** — Ohio was one of the leading US wine states in the nineteenth century before later disruptions.

name: San Juan
description:
**San Juan** is Argentina's second-largest wine province, sitting in the arid west just north of Mendoza at the foot of the Andes.

**Wines & grapes** — It is known for Syrah, which thrives in the heat, along with Bonarda, Malbec, and the aromatic white grape Torrontés. The region also has a long tradition of table grapes and brandy production.

**Character** — This is a hot, dry, high-altitude desert irrigated by Andean meltwater, yielding ripe, deeply coloured, full-bodied reds with soft tannins. Elevation and cool nights help retain some freshness.

**Good to know** — San Juan is often cited as one of the warmer, more sun-baked corners of Argentine wine country.

name: Wairarapa
description:
**Wairarapa** is a small but respected wine region at the southern tip of New Zealand's North Island, centred on the town of Martinborough.

**Wines & grapes** — It built its name on Pinot Noir, producing structured, savoury reds, and also makes fine aromatic whites such as Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris and Riesling. Production is boutique in scale.

**Character** — A cool, dry climate with free-draining river-terrace soils and marked day-night temperature swings gives wines of concentration, firm structure and vibrant acidity. The Pinot Noir often shows dark cherry, spice and earthy depth.

**Good to know** — Despite tiny volumes, Wairarapa (and Martinborough in particular) sits among New Zealand's most highly regarded Pinot Noir zones.

name: King Valley, Victoria
description:
**King Valley, Victoria** is an alpine wine region in northeast Victoria, Australia, rising from valley floor into the foothills of the Great Dividing Range.

**Wines & grapes** — It is best known for Italian varieties, especially sparkling Prosecco (Glera) and reds like Sangiovese, Nebbiolo and Barbera, reflecting the area's strong Italian settler heritage. Cool-climate whites are also made.

**Character** — Vineyards span a wide range of elevations, so styles shift from riper, fuller wines lower down to fresher, higher-acid wines up in the hills. The overall signature is cool-climate freshness and food-friendly structure.

**Good to know** — The King Valley is often called the home of Australian Prosecco.

name: Victoria
description:
**Victoria** is a diverse wine state in southeastern Australia, home to more distinct wine regions than any other part of the country.

**Wines & grapes** — Its range is enormous: cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from areas like the Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula, peppery Shiraz from central Victoria, and rich fortified "stickies" (Muscat and Topaque) from Rutherglen in the northeast.

**Character** — Climates run from cool coastal and alpine zones to warm inland districts, so no single style defines the state; elegance and regional variety are the through-line. Many of Australia's most refined cool-climate wines come from here.

**Good to know** — Rutherglen's fortified Muscats are among the world's greatest sweet wines.

name: Azores
description:
**Azores** is a remote Portuguese archipelago in the mid-Atlantic, where vines grow in one of the most dramatic wine landscapes anywhere.

**Wines & grapes** — Production centres on distinctive whites from grapes such as Verdelho, Arinto dos Açores and Terrantez do Pico, giving mineral, saline, sometimes briny wines. Volumes are small and largely artisanal.

**Character** — Vines are often planted in small stone-walled enclosures on black volcanic basalt to shelter them from wind and sea spray, and the wines carry a hallmark salty, volcanic minerality with brisk acidity.

**Good to know** — The historic vineyard landscape on Pico Island is recognised for its striking lava-stone walls.

name: North Carolina
description:
**North Carolina** is a wine-producing state in the southeastern United States, straddling both a native-grape tradition near the coast and a growing vinifera scene in the hills of the west.

**Wines & grapes** — The historic style is sweet wine from native muscadine grapes, especially the bronze Scuppernong. Cooler upland areas increasingly grow European varieties such as Cabernet, Merlot, Chardonnay and Viognier, along with hybrids.

**Character** — The state spans a warm, humid coastal plain and cooler foothills of the Blue Ridge and Yadkin Valley, so styles range from soft, fruity muscadine wines to drier, more structured bottlings inland. It remains a small, regionally focused industry rather than a national force.

name: Vaud
description:
**Vaud** is a canton in western Switzerland and one of the country's most important wine regions, wrapped around the northern shore of Lake Geneva and the Rhône valley.

**Wines & grapes** — White wine dominates, built almost entirely on Chasselas, which here gives dry, delicate, mineral wines. Reds and rosés come mainly from Pinot Noir and Gamay.

**Character** — The famous Lavaux terraces, stone-walled vineyards tumbling down to the lake, benefit from a triple reflection of sunlight from sky, water and walls. The wines are typically light, fresh and food-friendly, prized locally and rarely exported in quantity.

**Good to know** — Chasselas from Vaud is often bottled by village, such as Dézaley or Épesses, each with its own reputation.

name: Tennessee
description:
**Tennessee** is a wine-producing state in the southeastern United States with a small but steadily developing industry spread across its varied terrain.

**Wines & grapes** — Wineries here work with native muscadine grapes, cold-hardy hybrids and, in favourable spots, European varieties. Sweeter and fruit wines remain common, though drier table wines are increasingly made.

**Character** — The climate is warm and humid, which suits robust native and hybrid vines more readily than delicate vinifera. Most production is aimed at local visitors and tasting rooms rather than wide distribution.

name: Kamptal
description:
**Kamptal** is a leading white-wine region in Lower Austria, taking its name from the Kamp, a small tributary of the Danube whose valley is centred on the town of Langenlois.

**Wines & grapes** — The signature wines are dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, ranging from bright everyday bottlings to age-worthy single-vineyard wines. Smaller amounts of other whites and some red are also produced.

**Character** — A meeting of warm Pannonian air and cool northern currents gives the wines both ripeness and lively acidity. The famous Heiligenstein hill, with its ancient desert-sandstone soils, produces some of Austria's most respected Rieslings.

**Good to know** — Kamptal uses the DAC system, which reserves the name for the region's typical Grüner Veltliner and Riesling styles.

name: Bairrada
description:
**Bairrada** is a wine region in central Portugal, set on clay-rich lowlands not far inland from the Atlantic coast between Coimbra and Aveiro.

**Wines & grapes** — It is best known for firm, structured reds from the local Baga grape, along with crisp whites and a strong tradition of traditional-method sparkling wine. Arinto, Bical and Maria Gomes are common white varieties.

**Character** — The maritime climate brings rain and cooling, so Baga ripens slowly and keeps high acidity and tannin, giving reds that can be austere young but reward patient cellaring. Chalky-clay soils reinforce the wines' freshness and longevity.

**Good to know** — Bairrada's sparkling wines are among Portugal's most highly regarded.

name: Aargau
description:
**Aargau** is a canton in northern Switzerland where vineyards follow the valleys of the Aare and Rhine rivers.

**Wines & grapes** — Pinot Noir, locally called Blauburgunder, is the leading red, while whites lean on Müller-Thurgau (often labelled Riesling-Silvaner) and Riesling. Production is on a modest scale.

**Character** — This is one of Switzerland's more northerly wine areas, so the climate is cool and the wines tend to be light, fresh and aromatic. Most is consumed within the country and rarely seen abroad.

name: Lyonnais
description:
**Lyonnais** is a small wine area in eastern France in the hills just west and south of the city of Lyon, sitting between Beaujolais to the north and the northern Rhône to the south.

**Wines & grapes** — The wines fall under the Coteaux du Lyonnais appellation. Reds and rosés are based on Gamay, while whites come mainly from Chardonnay and Aligoté.

**Character** — Sharing granite-influenced soils and a Gamay tradition with neighbouring Beaujolais, the reds are bright, juicy and made for early drinking. It is a low-profile region whose wines are mostly enjoyed locally around Lyon.

name: Mittelrhein
description:
**Mittelrhein** is a scenic German wine region running along the steep gorge of the Rhine, roughly between Bingen and Koblenz, where the river cuts through slate hillsides dotted with castles.

**Wines & grapes** — Riesling is by far the dominant grape, giving racy, mineral whites, with some Pinot Noir (Spätburgunder) and other varieties in smaller amounts.

**Character** — Vines cling to precipitous slate terraces that soak up heat and drain well, producing Rieslings with vivid acidity and pronounced stony character. It is one of Germany's smaller wine regions, and the difficult terrain means much is worked by hand.

**Good to know** — The Rhine gorge here is a UNESCO World Heritage site, celebrated as much for its landscape as its wine.

name: Baden-Württemberg
description:
**Baden-Württemberg** is a federal state in southwestern Germany that encompasses two of the country's notable wine regions, Baden and Württemberg.

**Wines & grapes** — Baden, warmer and further south, is known for ripe Pinot family wines, including Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) and the Pinot Blanc and Gris family, plus Müller-Thurgau. Württemberg is unusually red-focused, with Trollinger and Lemberger among its mainstays.

**Character** — As an administrative rather than a single winemaking area, it covers a broad span of climates and soils, from the sun-warmed Rhine plain near the Kaiserstuhl to the cooler Neckar valley. Together the two regions make Germany a more red-friendly country than its Riesling image suggests.

name: Württemberg
description:
**Württemberg** is a wine region in southwestern Germany centred on the Neckar valley and its tributaries around Stuttgart and Heilbronn.

**Wines & grapes** — Unusually for Germany, it is a red-dominated region. Trollinger is the traditional local red, joined by Lemberger (Blaufränkisch), Schwarzriesling (Pinot Meunier) and Spätburgunder, alongside white Riesling.

**Character** — Vineyards on warm valley slopes give reds that are typically soft, approachable and often enjoyed young and locally, with Lemberger producing the more structured, ageable examples. Much of the output is consumed within the region, where wine is a strong part of everyday culture.

**Good to know** — Trollinger is something of a regional institution, tied closely to Swabian identity.

name: Corsica
description:
**Corsica** is a mountainous Mediterranean island belonging to France, lying between the mainland and Italy, with a wine culture shaped by both influences.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds and rosés rely on Nielluccio (closely related to Sangiovese) and the spicy Sciaccarello, while the aromatic Vermentino leads the whites. Rosé accounts for a large share of production.

**Character** — Abundant sunshine, sea breezes and diverse granite and limestone soils give wines that are warm and herb-scented, echoing the island's wild maquis scrubland. Appellations such as Patrimonio and Ajaccio are among the most respected.

**Good to know** — Corsica also has a tradition of sweet Muscat, notably Muscat du Cap Corse.

name: West Sussex
description:
**West Sussex** is a county in southern England and part of the country's celebrated cool-climate sparkling-wine scene, sitting on the chalk of the South Downs.

**Wines & grapes** — The focus is on traditional-method sparkling wine from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, alongside some still whites.

**Character** — A cool climate and chalky soils, geologically similar to those of Champagne, preserve the high acidity that gives these sparkling wines their crisp, fresh, mineral style. The county is home to several of England's best-known sparkling-wine producers.

name: Auckland
description:
**Auckland** ... — a wine region on New Zealand's North Island, wrapped around the country's largest city and reaching out to nearby islands like Waiheke. It is small in output but historically important, home to some of the country's oldest wineries.

**Wines & grapes** — a warm-climate mix leaning toward Bordeaux reds such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc, along with Syrah and Chardonnay. Waiheke Island in particular has built a reputation for structured red blends.

**Character** — the maritime climate is humid and comparatively warm for New Zealand, which favours later-ripening varieties that struggle further south. Wines tend to be riper and rounder than the crisp Sauvignon Blanc most people associate with the country, and boutique scale keeps volumes modest.

name: Trentino
description:
**Trentino** ... — a mountainous region in northern Italy, forming the southern half of the Trentino-Alto Adige area around the city of Trento. Alpine valleys and the influence of Lake Garda shape a wide range of styles.

**Wines & grapes** — whites from Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay and the local Nosiola, reds from Teroldego, Marzemino, Lagrein and international varieties, plus a strong tradition of traditional-method sparkling wine (Trentodoc) built on Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

**Character** — cool mountain air and big day-to-night temperature swings give the wines bright acidity and freshness. Elevation and the moderating lake produce clean, aromatic whites and lively sparkling wines, while Teroldego offers a deeper, dark-fruited red from the Campo Rotaliano plain.

name: North Coast, California
description:
**North Coast, California** ... — a large appellation in the United States covering the coastal counties north of San Francisco Bay, including Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino and Lake. It is one of California's most celebrated quality wine zones.

**Wines & grapes** — a broad span of styles, led by Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay, with important Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc, plus sparkling wine in cooler pockets.

**Character** — the defining factor is the Pacific: coastal fog and cool ocean air funnel inland, tempering the warm California sun and stretching out ripening. That range of microclimates, from foggy coastal ridges to warm inland valleys, lets the region make everything from crisp whites to powerful, age-worthy reds.

**Good to know** — as an umbrella appellation it spans many famous smaller districts, so a North Coast label points to origin more than a single specific style.

name: Basilicata
description:
**Basilicata** ... — a small, mountainous region in the arch of southern Italy's "boot," better known for rugged landscapes than for large-scale wine. Its reputation rests largely on the volcanic slopes of Mount Vulture.

**Wines & grapes** — the flagship is Aglianico, especially Aglianico del Vulture, a dark, structured red grown on volcanic soils. Smaller amounts of white and other reds are also made.

**Character** — high altitude and cool nights slow ripening, giving Aglianico here firm tannins, bright acidity and real ageing potential. The volcanic terrain lends a savoury, mineral edge, and the wines are often compared to the more famous Aglianico of neighbouring Campania while keeping their own rustic, earthy identity.

name: North Coast
description:
**North Coast** ... — a wine region in the United States, referring to the coastal counties of California north of San Francisco Bay, home to renowned areas such as Napa, Sonoma and Mendocino. It is among the country's premier fine-wine zones.

**Wines & grapes** — an extensive range topped by Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay, alongside Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc.

**Character** — cool marine air and fog off the Pacific moderate what would otherwise be a hot climate, creating many distinct microclimates within one large appellation. The result runs from bright, fresh whites and elegant Pinot Noir near the coast to rich, structured Cabernet in warmer inland valleys.

name: Uco Valley
description:
**Uco Valley** ... — a high-altitude wine region in Argentina's Mendoza province, spreading across the foothills of the Andes to the south of Mendoza city. It has become one of the country's most exciting sources of premium wine.

**Wines & grapes** — Malbec is king, but the cool elevation also suits Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and aromatic whites, with fresh, high-toned styles increasingly the signature.

**Character** — vineyards planted well above a thousand metres enjoy intense sunlight by day and cold nights, which preserves acidity and builds colour and aromatics. Stony, alluvial soils and the altitude give Uco Malbec more freshness, floral lift and firm structure than warmer, lower Mendoza sites.

**Good to know** — the valley's cooler, higher plots have driven Argentina's move toward more elegant, terroir-focused wines.

name: Illinois
description:
**Illinois** ... — a wine-producing state in the American Midwest, with a small industry spread mainly across river valleys and rural districts rather than one concentrated hub.

**Wines & grapes** — production centres on cold-hardy grapes suited to the climate, including the French-American hybrids Chambourcin, Vidal Blanc and Seyval Blanc and the native American Norton, made in a range from dry to sweet.

**Character** — a continental climate with hot summers and cold winters favours grapes bred to survive frost, so hybrids dominate over classic European vinifera. Most wineries are modest, family-run operations serving local visitors, and the wines are generally approachable and made for early drinking.

name: Dão
description:
**Dão** ... — a historic wine region in north-central Portugal, set in a granite plateau ringed by mountains that shelter it from coastal and continental extremes. It is one of the country's classic sources of refined red wine.

**Wines & grapes** — reds built around Touriga Nacional, with Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Alfrocheiro and Jaen, plus fresh whites led by the Encruzado grape.

**Character** — granite soils, altitude and a protected climate give the reds firm structure, elegance and the ability to age gracefully, often described as more restrained and perfumed than the bolder wines of the nearby Douro. Encruzado, meanwhile, makes some of Portugal's finest dry whites.

**Good to know** — long regarded alongside the Douro as one of Portugal's benchmark table-wine regions.

name: Wisconsin
description:
**Wisconsin** ... — a wine-producing state in the northern United States, with a small, dispersed industry shaped by its cold Midwestern climate.

**Wines & grapes** — the emphasis is on cold-hardy hybrids such as Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent and St. Croix, many developed to withstand harsh winters, along with fruit wines including the state's well-known cranberry wines.

**Character** — long, freezing winters rule out most classic European vinifera, so growers rely on hybrids bred for survival and short seasons. Wineries are typically small and tourism-focused, and the wines range from crisp and dry to distinctly sweet, often reflecting local fruit as much as grapes.

name: Rapel Valley
description:
**Rapel Valley** ... — a large and important wine region in Chile, lying in the country's Central Valley south of Santiago. It splits into two well-known sub-zones, Cachapoal to the north and Colchagua to the south.

**Wines & grapes** — red-dominant, famed for Carménère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, with Colchagua in particular known for rich, ripe reds.

**Character** — a warm, sunny Mediterranean climate with reliable dry summers ripens red grapes fully, while cooling influences from the Andes and, in places, the Pacific help retain balance. The wines are typically generous, deeply coloured and fruit-forward, with Carménère offering the plummy, herbal signature that has become a Chilean calling card.

**Good to know** — Colchagua's premium reds have done much to build Chile's international reputation.

name: McLaren Vale
description:
**McLaren Vale** ... — a warm coastal wine region in South Australia, just south of Adelaide near the Gulf St Vincent. It is one of Australia's most respected sources of full-bodied red wine.

**Wines & grapes** — Shiraz and Grenache are the stars, joined by Cabernet Sauvignon and a growing cast of Mediterranean varieties such as Mourvèdre, Tempranillo and Fiano suited to the climate.

**Character** — a Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers cooled by afternoon sea breezes yields ripe, generous reds with soft tannins and rich, dark fruit. Old bush-vine Grenache and diverse soils give real depth, and the region has embraced sustainable and organic farming.

**Good to know** — its old-vine Grenache is increasingly prized as one of Australia's finest expressions of the grape.

name: Columbia Valley
description:
**Columbia Valley** ... — a vast wine region in the northwestern United States, covering much of eastern Washington and reaching into Oregon along the Columbia River. It is the backbone of Washington State's wine industry.

**Wines & grapes** — a broad, balanced range led by Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah among reds, with Riesling, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc among whites.

**Character** — sheltered from Pacific rain by the Cascade Mountains, this high desert sees hot, sunny days and cold nights, plus long summer daylight at its northern latitude. That combination ripens grapes fully while preserving acidity, giving reds both power and freshness, and irrigation from the river makes viticulture possible in an otherwise arid landscape.

**Good to know** — it is an umbrella appellation containing many notable smaller districts.

name: Balearic Islands
description:
**Balearic Islands** are Spain's Mediterranean archipelago east of the mainland, with most winemaking concentrated on Mallorca and a smaller presence on Menorca, Ibiza and Formentera.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds and rosés lead, built on native grapes such as Manto Negro and Callet, often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah or Tempranillo. Whites come from local varieties like Prensal Blanc (Moll), alongside Chardonnay and Muscat. Mallorca's main quality zones are the DOs Binissalem and Pla i Llevant.

**Character** — A warm, sunny, sea-tempered climate gives ripe, generous, easy-drinking wines. The islands have shifted from bulk output toward small estates reviving indigenous grapes, so bottlings can show real local personality.

**Good to know** — Production is tiny and much of it is drunk on the islands, so bottles are a fun find for travellers and collectors of unusual Spanish wines.

name: Langhorne Creek
description:
**Langhorne Creek** is a warm, flat wine region in South Australia, southeast of Adelaide near Lake Alexandrina, long prized as a source of soft, ripe fruit.

**Wines & grapes** — It is red-wine country above all, best known for plush Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, with Malbec, Merlot and some white varieties also grown.

**Character** — Cooling afternoon breezes off the nearby lake moderate the heat and stretch out ripening, giving supple, rounded reds with sweet dark fruit and gentle tannins. Historically many grapes were sold to big producers for blending, but the region now has a growing number of estate wines under its own name.

**Good to know** — The vineyards were traditionally watered by seasonal flooding of the Bremer and Angas rivers, an unusual natural irrigation that shaped the district's reputation for reliable, generous crops.

name: Texas Hill Country
description:
**Texas Hill Country** is a large wine region in central Texas, spreading across the rolling limestone hills west of Austin and San Antonio, and one of the anchors of the state's fast-growing wine scene.

**Wines & grapes** — Growers have leaned into warm-climate, Mediterranean and Rhône grapes that suit the heat, including Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Grenache and Sangiovese for reds, and Viognier, Roussanne and Blanc du Bois among whites. Tannat and Cabernet Sauvignon also feature.

**Character** — Hot days, cooler nights and limestone-rich soils give ripe, full-bodied wines. Late frosts, hail and heat make it a challenging place to farm, so quality varies, but the best producers make characterful, food-friendly bottlings.

**Good to know** — It is a popular tasting-room destination and a big driver of Texas wine tourism.

name: Queensland
description:
**Queensland** is Australia's warm northeastern state, a smaller and less-known wine producer than the southern states but with a growing craft scene.

**Wines & grapes** — A wide mix of varieties is grown, including Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot for reds and Chardonnay, Verdelho and Semillon for whites, plus a taste for alternative Mediterranean grapes.

**Character** — Most serious vineyards sit at altitude to escape the subtropical heat, giving fresher, more balanced wines than the lowland climate would suggest. The best-known quality zone is the elevated Granite Belt in the state's south.

**Good to know** — Much of the wine is enjoyed locally and by visitors, making Queensland bottles an uncommon sight elsewhere.

name: Granite Belt, Queensland
description:
**Granite Belt, Queensland** is the state's leading wine region, a high, cool plateau around Stanthorpe near the New South Wales border, named for its coarse granite soils.

**Wines & grapes** — Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot lead the reds, with Chardonnay, Verdelho and Semillon among the whites. The region is also known for championing unusual "alternative" varieties such as Tempranillo, Fiano and Durif.

**Character** — At around 800 metres and higher, elevation brings cold nights and a genuine growing-season chill that keeps the wines fresh and structured despite Queensland's warm reputation. The decomposed-granite, sandy soils drain freely and add a lean, mineral edge.

**Good to know** — Its "Strange Bird" trail celebrates lesser-known grapes, giving the region a distinct identity within Australian wine.

name: West Flanders
description:
**West Flanders** is a coastal province in the north of Belgium, part of the country's small but slowly expanding cool-climate wine scene.

**Wines & grapes** — Production is limited and geared to fresh whites and sparkling wines, typically from cool-climate and disease-resistant grape varieties suited to a northern maritime setting.

**Character** — The cool, damp, Atlantic-influenced climate makes for light, crisp, high-acid wines, and winemaking here is a niche, artisanal pursuit rather than a large industry. Bottles are made in tiny quantities and rarely travel far from home.

name: Savoie
description:
**Savoie** is an alpine wine region in eastern France, tucked among the mountains and lakes near the Swiss and Italian borders, famous for crisp, high-altitude whites.

**Wines & grapes** — Whites dominate, chiefly from Jacquère, along with Altesse (also called Roussette), Roussanne (known locally as Bergeron in Chignin) and Chasselas. Reds and rosés come mainly from Mondeuse, Gamay and Pinot Noir.

**Character** — A cool mountain climate and stony, often limestone slopes give light-bodied, bright, refreshing wines with lively acidity and an almost saline, mineral snap. Most are meant to be drunk young.

**Good to know** — Savoie wines pair naturally with alpine cheese dishes like fondue and raclette, and much of the output is enjoyed in the region's ski resorts.

name: Willamette Valley, Oregon
description:
**Willamette Valley, Oregon** is one of the Pacific Northwest's most celebrated wine regions, stretching south of Portland in the northwest United States, and one of the world's benchmark homes for cool-climate Pinot Noir.

**Wines & grapes** — Pinot Noir is the signature grape, producing elegant, perfumed reds. Whites are led by Pinot Gris and Chardonnay, with Riesling and sparkling wine also important.

**Character** — A cool, wet, marine-influenced climate and a long, gentle ripening season give wines of finesse, bright acidity and restraint rather than sheer power. Soils range from volcanic "Jory" red basalt to marine sedimentary types, and terroir-focused sub-AVAs like the Dundee Hills and Eola-Amity Hills are prized.

**Good to know** — Its cool, damp autumns make vintages variable, rewarding careful growers and giving each year its own character.

name: Monterey County
description:
**Monterey County** is a major coastal wine region on California's Central Coast, running inland along the Salinas Valley south of Monterey Bay.

**Wines & grapes** — Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are the calling cards, with Riesling, Pinot Gris, Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon also widely planted. Cooler northern zones favour whites and Pinot, while warmer inland stretches ripen fuller reds.

**Character** — Cold ocean air and strong afternoon winds funnel down the valley from the bay, dramatically cooling the vineyards and extending ripening, which builds vivid acidity and bright fruit. The county spans a wide range of sites, from breezy valley floors to the hillside Santa Lucia Highlands.

**Good to know** — The Santa Lucia Highlands sub-appellation is especially esteemed for concentrated, sought-after Pinot Noir and Syrah.

name: Lisboa
description:
**Lisboa** is a large coastal wine region in west-central Portugal, running up the Atlantic seaboard north of the capital, and formerly known as Estremadura.

**Wines & grapes** — It is one of Portugal's most productive regions, making reds, whites and rosés across many styles. Native grapes lead, including Castelão, Touriga Nacional and Aragonez (Tempranillo) for reds and Arinto, Fernão Pires and Vital for whites.

**Character** — The cooling, sometimes windy Atlantic influence keeps many wines fresh and bright, and much of the output is well-priced, everyday drinking. Nested inside are distinctive smaller DOCs such as Bucelas for crisp Arinto whites, historic Colares grown in coastal sands, and Alenquer and Óbidos for reds.

**Good to know** — Its blend of high volume and pockets of tradition makes it a great source of value and discovery.

name: Valle d'Aosta
description:
**Valle d'Aosta** is Italy's smallest wine region, a narrow alpine valley in the far northwest, ringed by the highest peaks of the Alps near the French and Swiss borders.

**Wines & grapes** — It grows a remarkable range of native and international grapes on steep terraces, including reds from Petit Rouge, Fumin and Nebbiolo (locally Picotendro or Picotener), and whites from Prié Blanc, Petite Arvine and Müller-Thurgau.

**Character** — Some of Europe's highest vineyards, cool mountain air and stony slopes give light, fresh, high-acid wines with real alpine character, often made in tiny quantities by growers farming by hand. Its single DOC, Valle d'Aosta, covers the whole valley.

**Good to know** — Prié Blanc from Morgex and La Salle ripens at extreme altitude on ungrafted vines, a mountain rarity.

name: Jumilla
description:
**Jumilla** is a warm, arid wine region in southeastern Spain, straddling the Murcia and Castilla-La Mancha border, celebrated as a stronghold of the Monastrell grape.

**Wines & grapes** — Powerful, dark reds from Monastrell (known elsewhere as Mourvèdre) are the signature, sometimes blended with Syrah, Tempranillo, Garnacha or Cabernet Sauvignon. Some fresh whites and rosés are also made.

**Character** — Baking sun, very low rainfall and high-altitude limestone soils concentrate the fruit, giving ripe, full-bodied reds with dark berry flavours, a warm herbal note and often generous alcohol. Old bush-trained vines add depth.

**Good to know** — Phylloxera reached Jumilla unusually late, its spread slowed by the region's sandy soils, and low-yielding old vines still make it a source of concentrated reds at excellent value.

name: Valencia
description:
**Valencia** is a wine region on Spain's eastern Mediterranean coast, centred on the port city of the same name and long a hub for both everyday bottlings and, increasingly, more serious wines from its higher inland hills.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds and rosés lean on Bobal, Monastrell and Tempranillo, while whites come from Merseguera, Macabeo and the aromatic Moscatel. The region is especially known for sweet Moscatel de Valencia, a fragrant, grapey dessert wine.

**Character** — The warm Mediterranean climate ripens grapes easily, giving generous, fruit-forward reds and juicy rosés, while cooler vineyards at altitude inland lend more freshness and structure. It offers reliable value across a wide spread of styles.

**Good to know** — Vineyards range from the coastal plain up into the Utiel-Requena plateau, so quality varies with elevation and site.

name: Castilla IGP
description:
**Castilla IGP** is a broad regional wine category covering the vast central plateau of Castilla-La Mancha in the heart of Spain, used for wines that fall outside the stricter appellation rules yet still show regional origin.

**Wines & grapes** — It spans reds, whites and rosés from a wide grape palette, including Tempranillo, Garnacha, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah for reds, and Airén, Verdejo and Sauvignon Blanc among the whites.

**Character** — This is high, dry, sun-baked country with a strongly continental climate of hot days and cold nights, producing ripe, approachable wines. The flexible IGP framework gives growers room to blend international and Spanish varieties, making it a common source of good-value everyday bottles.

name: La Mancha
description:
**La Mancha** is a huge wine region on the arid central plateau south of Madrid, one of the largest single denominated vineyard areas in the world and historically the engine of Spain's bulk wine output.

**Wines & grapes** — The white Airén, planted across enormous acreage, remains a mainstay, while reds increasingly rely on Tempranillo (locally called Cencibel), alongside Garnacha, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.

**Character** — The climate is fiercely continental, with scorching summers, cold winters and very little rain, which keeps yields naturally in check and concentrates flavour. Modern winemaking has lifted quality considerably, and the region now turns out clean, fruity, affordable reds and whites.

**Good to know** — The name is forever tied to Don Quixote's windswept plains.

name: Styria
description:
**Styria** (Steiermark) is a wine region in the green, hilly southeast of Austria, close to the Slovenian border, celebrated above all for crisp, aromatic white wines.

**Wines & grapes** — Sauvignon Blanc is the star, joined by Welschriesling, Morillon (the local name for Chardonnay), Weissburgunder and Muskateller. The western part is also known for Schilcher, a sharp rosé made from the Blauer Wildbacher grape.

**Character** — Steep slopes, a mild but variable climate and diverse soils give whites of bright acidity, clarity and vivid fruit and herb aromatics. The wines are typically dry, lively and food-friendly, prized for their freshness rather than power.

name: Castile and León
description:
**Castile and León** is a large region across the high plains of north-central Spain, drained by the Duero river and home to several of the country's most prestigious wine appellations.

**Wines & grapes** — It is red-wine country at heart, with Tempranillo (known locally as Tinta del País or Tinta de Toro) driving the powerful reds of Ribera del Duero and Toro, and Mencía shaping the fresher reds of Bierzo. For whites, Verdejo from Rueda is the signature.

**Character** — High altitude and a harsh continental climate of hot days and cold nights build deeply coloured, structured reds with firm tannins and good acidity.

**Good to know** — Some of Spain's most sought-after wines come from within its borders.

name: Durbanville
description:
**Durbanville** is a cool-climate ward on the hills just north of Cape Town in South Africa's Coastal Region, benefiting from breezes and mist off the nearby Atlantic.

**Wines & grapes** — It has built a strong reputation for Sauvignon Blanc, and also produces good Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and other whites.

**Character** — Ocean influence tempers the summer heat, and the rolling clay-rich slopes hold moisture well, giving whites with zesty acidity and pronounced green, herbal and tropical notes. The reds tend to be firm and cool-fruited rather than jammy.

name: Constantia
description:
**Constantia** is a historic ward on the eastern slopes of the Cape Peninsula near Cape Town, one of the oldest wine-growing districts in the Southern Hemisphere and famous for centuries for its sweet wine.

**Wines & grapes** — Its legendary product was Vin de Constance, a lusciously sweet Muscat once prized by European royalty. Today Sauvignon Blanc leads the modern lineup, alongside other whites and some elegant reds.

**Character** — Cool sea breezes off False Bay and well-drained mountain soils give wines of freshness, precision and finesse. The Sauvignon Blancs are aromatic and racy, while the revived sweet Muscat remains a sought-after specialty.

**Good to know** — Winemaking here dates back to the late 17th century.

name: Cerdon
description:
**Cerdon** is a small area within the Bugey region of eastern France, in the foothills between the Jura and Savoie, best known for a distinctive pink sparkling wine.

**Wines & grapes** — Its signature is Bugey-Cerdon, a lightly sparkling, off-dry rosé made mainly from Gamay with some Poulsard, produced by the ancestral method where fermentation finishes in the bottle.

**Character** — The wine is delicately fizzy, pale pink, low in alcohol and gently sweet, with fresh red-berry and floral flavours. It is an easygoing, aromatic sparkler meant to be drunk young and well chilled.

name: Auvergne
description:
**Auvergne** is a wine area in the volcanic heart of central France, in the Massif Central along the upper reaches of the Allier, producing wines under the Côtes d'Auvergne name.

**Wines & grapes** — Gamay dominates the light, juicy reds and rosés, with Pinot Noir also planted, while Chardonnay accounts for the whites.

**Character** — Volcanic and granitic soils, combined with a cool, hilly climate, give reds that are fresh, bright and relatively light-bodied, with vivid red fruit and a mineral edge. The wines are honest, drinkable and closer in spirit to Beaujolais and the Loire than to richer southern styles.

name: Calabria
description:
**Calabria** forms the mountainous "toe" of southern Italy, a warm, sun-drenched region with a long winemaking history stretching back to ancient Greek settlers.

**Wines & grapes** — The red Gaglioppo grape is the region's calling card, most famously in the wines of Cirò, while Magliocco adds to the reds and Greco Bianco supplies aromatic whites and sweet specialties.

**Character** — Hot Mediterranean sunshine tempered by cooling mountain elevation yields reds that are firm, savoury and full of dark and red fruit, often with an earthy, herbal streak. Historically overlooked, Calabria is increasingly recognised for characterful wines from native grapes.

**Good to know** — Greek colonists brought vines to these shores over two millennia ago.

name: Córdoba
description:
**Córdoba** is a province in central Argentina where winemaking, once widespread historically, is enjoying a modern revival in the high valleys of the Sierras.

**Wines & grapes** — Growers work with a mix of varieties, including Malbec and other reds along with aromatic whites, reflecting the country's broad grape palette rather than a single specialty.

**Character** — Vineyards planted at altitude in the mountain valleys benefit from strong sunshine, cool nights and clean air, which help preserve acidity and freshness in the wines. As an emerging region, its output is small but growing, driven by a wave of boutique producers exploring the terroir.

name: Central Victoria
description:
**Central Victoria** is a wine zone in the state of Victoria, southeastern Australia, taking in respected districts such as Heathcote, Bendigo, Goulburn Valley, Nagambie Lakes and the Strathbogie Ranges.

**Wines & grapes** — Shiraz is the flagship, especially the deep, rich reds of Heathcote grown on ancient Cambrian soils. Cabernet Sauvignon adds structure, while the Nagambie area is known for distinctive whites from Marsanne and Riesling.

**Character** — A generally warm, continental climate moderated by elevation produces reds of ripe, generous dark fruit, good concentration and velvety texture. The zone balances powerful, age-worthy reds with elegant, long-lived whites.

**Good to know** — Heathcote's red soils are prized by Shiraz specialists worldwide.

name: Citrusdal Berg
description:
**Citrusdal Berg** is a ward in South Africa's Western Cape, set in the rugged Cederberg mountains of the wider Olifants River region, well to the north of Cape Town.

**Wines & grapes** — Chenin Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc anchor the whites, alongside reds such as Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon grown on the warmer, better-drained slopes.

**Character** — The defining feature is altitude: some of the vineyards here sit among the highest in the country, where cool mountain nights and stony, sandstone-derived soils help the grapes hold onto freshness and acidity despite the dry, sun-drenched growing season.

**Good to know** — The remote, high-lying sites have earned the area a reputation for elegant, mineral wines that punch above the region's small size.

name: Bretagne
description:
**Bretagne** — better known in English as Brittany — is a peninsula in the far northwest of France, jutting into the Atlantic with a cool, wet, maritime climate.

**Wines & grapes** — It has never been a classic wine region and is far better known for cider, while the Muscadet vineyards lie just to its south in the Loire. A modern, small-scale revival has seen a handful of growers plant vines, often favouring early-ripening and disease-tolerant varieties suited to the damp climate.

**Character** — Cool temperatures, frequent rain and a short growing season make ripening a challenge, so what wine is made tends to be light and crisp. Production remains tiny and experimental rather than established.

name: Extremadura
description:
**Extremadura** is a large, sparsely populated region in western Spain, bordering Portugal, with its vineyards concentrated in the Ribera del Guadiana appellation around the Guadiana river.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds are led by Tempranillo (locally called Cencibel) and Garnacha, while whites draw on native varieties such as Pardina and Cayetana Blanca; the area has long supplied large volumes of everyday wine.

**Character** — The climate is hot, dry and strongly continental, with baking summers that ripen grapes easily and yield generous, ripe, approachable styles. Long a source of bulk and distilling wine, it has gradually shifted toward more quality-focused bottlings while remaining one of Spain's better-value corners.

name: Hessen
description:
**Hessen** is a federal state in western Germany. Its vineyards fall mainly within two officially designated wine regions: the celebrated Rheingau along the Rhine, and the small Hessische Bergstraße further east.

**Wines & grapes** — Riesling is the signature grape, producing everything from bone-dry to lusciously sweet whites, with Pinot varieties (Spätburgunder and the Pinot Blanc/Gris family) also grown.

**Character** — The best sites, especially in the Rheingau, sit on south-facing slopes above the river, where reflected warmth and slate or loess soils give Rieslings their trademark balance of ripe fruit, racy acidity and mineral cut.

**Good to know** — Note that Rheinhessen, despite the similar name, lies in the neighbouring state of Rhineland-Palatinate, not in Hessen.

name: Lower Rhine (Niederrhein)
description:
**Lower Rhine (Niederrhein)** is a region in western Germany following the Rhine as it flows north toward the Dutch border, beyond the traditional heartland of German viticulture.

**Wines & grapes** — This is very marginal wine country rather than an established region; the cool, northerly climate favours what little is grown here toward early-ripening white varieties and light styles.

**Character** — Sitting well north of Germany's classic vineyards, it has a cool, damp climate that makes fully ripening grapes difficult, so viticulture remains small-scale and modern rather than historically significant. Any wine produced tends to be light and fresh.

name: Thrace
description:
**Thrace** is a major wine region in southern Bulgaria, spread across the warm Thracian lowlands and one of the country's most important and historic zones for winemaking, a tradition stretching back to antiquity.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds dominate, built around the native Mavrud grape prized for its depth and structure, alongside international varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, plus local crossings like Rubin.

**Character** — A warm, sunny continental climate tempered by surrounding hills gives ripe, full-bodied reds with good colour and firm tannins. The area blends deep-rooted local grapes with modern international styles.

**Good to know** — The ancient Thracians who gave the region its name were among Europe's earliest wine cultures.

name: Crimea
description:
**Crimea** is a Black Sea peninsula, part of Ukraine, with a long winemaking heritage centred on its southern coast.

**Wines & grapes** — It is most famous for fortified and sweet dessert wines in the styles of Port, Madeira and Muscat, produced most notably at the historic Massandra cellars, as well as sparkling wine associated with the Novyi Svit house. Both native and international grapes are grown.

**Character** — The sheltered southern coastline enjoys a mild, near-Mediterranean climate protected by mountains, ideal for ripening grapes to the high sugar levels that its rich, long-lived fortified wines require.

**Good to know** — The Massandra collection holds one of the world's most storied libraries of aged fortified wines.

name: Snowy Mountains
description:
**Snowy Mountains** is a high-altitude wine zone in the alpine country of New South Wales, in southeastern Australia.

**Wines & grapes** — As a cool, elevated region it leans toward aromatic whites and cool-climate styles, along with fruit suited to sparkling-wine bases; plantings here are limited.

**Character** — Defined by its elevation and mountain setting, the area has a genuinely cool climate with cold nights and a long, slow ripening season, which helps grapes retain bright acidity and fresh, restrained flavours. It remains a small and specialised corner of Australian viticulture.

name: Crete
description:
**Crete** is the largest of the Greek islands, lying in the southern Aegean, with a winemaking history reaching back thousands of years to some of Europe's earliest wine cultures.

**Wines & grapes** — The island is a treasury of indigenous grapes: whites like Vidiano, Vilana and Thrapsathiri, and reds such as Kotsifali, Mandilaria and the age-worthy Liatiko. Several appellations, including Peza, Archanes, Dafnes and Sitia, formalise these traditions.

**Character** — The Mediterranean climate is warm and sunny, but mountain vineyards and cooling sea breezes lend the wines balance and aromatic lift. A modern revival has refocused Crete on its distinctive native varieties.

**Good to know** — Liatiko-based wines, sometimes sweet, are among the island's most characterful and long-lived reds.

name: Secano Interior, Maule Valley
description:
**Secano Interior, Maule Valley** refers to the dry-farmed interior of Chile's Maule Valley, in the country's Central Valley south of Santiago, where old vines grow on the hills between the coastal range and the central plain.

**Wines & grapes** — The area is celebrated for old, unirrigated bush vines, above all País and Carignan, which yield concentrated, characterful reds; the local Carignan has become a flagship for the wider Maule.

**Character** — "Secano" means dry-farmed, and these gnarled, low-yielding vines survive on rainfall alone in granite-rich soils, producing rustic yet vibrant reds with deep colour, firm structure and bright acidity that reflect their old-vine heritage.

name: Maule Valley
description:
**Maule Valley** is one of Chile's largest and oldest wine regions, sitting in the southern part of the Central Valley, a few hours south of Santiago.

**Wines & grapes** — It grows a broad palette, from Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot to the historic País, but has earned recent acclaim for old-vine Carignan, often made from dry-farmed bush vines.

**Character** — A warm Mediterranean climate with cool, wetter conditions than regions further north, plus a wealth of ungrafted, unirrigated old vines, gives Maule reds real depth, freshness and a sense of place.

**Good to know** — A growers' movement has spotlighted the valley's ancient dry-farmed Carignan as one of Chile's most distinctive expressions.

name: Wakayama
description:
**Wakayama** is a prefecture on Japan's Kii Peninsula, south of Osaka, facing the Pacific with a warm, humid climate.

**Wines & grapes** — It is far better known for fruit growing — citrus such as mikan and ume plums — than for wine, and grape-wine production is small and local in scale.

**Character** — The warm, rainy climate is challenging for viticulture, so what wine is made is produced on a modest, artisanal basis rather than as part of an established regional industry.

name: Akita
description:
**Akita** is a prefecture in northern Japan, on the Sea of Japan side of the Tohoku region. It is far better known for rice and premium sake than for wine, though a handful of small wineries work in its cool northern climate.

**Wines & grapes** — Output is limited and artisanal, typically light reds, whites and rosés from cold-hardy hybrids and adaptable vinifera grapes suited to short, cool growing seasons.

**Character** — This is a marginal, snowy climate for the vine, so the wines tend to be fresh and modest in scale, made in tiny quantities by growers experimenting at the northern edge of Japanese viticulture.

name: Norrland
description:
**Norrland** is the vast northern portion of Sweden, a cold, sparsely populated area stretching toward the Arctic. It sits at the extreme frontier of grape growing and produces only a trickle of wine.

**Wines & grapes** — Any wine here comes from cold-hardy hybrid grapes, and fruit and berry wines are more common than grape wine in such a climate.

**Character** — With short summers, long daylight and harsh winters, the region is a challenging place for the vine; expect small-scale, experimental production rather than an established wine tradition.

name: Atlas Mountains
description:
**Atlas Mountains** refers to the mountain range running through Morocco, where vineyards planted at altitude escape some of the heat of the surrounding lowlands. It is part of Morocco's modest but long-standing wine scene.

**Wines & grapes** — The focus is on reds and rosés, generally from French-origin varieties such as Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache and Syrah, styles rooted in the country's Mediterranean and colonial-era history.

**Character** — Elevation brings cooler nights and a wider day-to-night temperature swing, helping the grapes keep freshness and colour in an otherwise warm, sun-drenched land.

name: Almaty
description:
**Almaty** is a region in southeastern Kazakhstan, centred on the country's largest city and set against the foothills of the Tian Shan mountains. It is one of Kazakhstan's established grape-growing areas.

**Wines & grapes** — Production covers reds and whites, drawing on international varieties along with grapes suited to the local continental conditions.

**Character** — A sharply continental climate with hot summers and cold winters, tempered by mountain foothills, shapes wines from a country whose viticulture is small but has deep Central Asian roots.

name: Southern Kazakhstan
description:
**Southern Kazakhstan** is a warm, southerly stretch of Kazakhstan and one of the country's principal areas for growing grapes. Viticulture here is aided by the milder winters relative to the country's north.

**Wines & grapes** — Both reds and whites are made, from a mix of international and locally grown varieties suited to the region's heat and long growing season.

**Character** — The climate is continental and sunny, giving ripe, generous fruit; wine here forms part of a Central Asian tradition that is small in scale but centuries old.

name: Zenata
description:
**Zenata** is a wine area on Morocco's Atlantic coast, near Casablanca, and one of the appellations within the country's system of protected origins. Its coastal setting sets it apart from Morocco's warmer interior.

**Wines & grapes** — The emphasis is on reds and rosés, chiefly from French-associated varieties such as Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache and Syrah.

**Character** — Cooling breezes off the Atlantic moderate the climate, helping the wines retain freshness; the region reflects Morocco's Mediterranean-influenced, French-shaped wine heritage.

name: Eastern Anatolia
description:
**Eastern Anatolia** is a high, rugged region in the east of Turkey and a heartland for the country's native grape varieties. It is one of the historic cradles of viticulture, in a part of the world where the vine has grown for millennia.

**Wines & grapes** — The area is closely tied to indigenous Turkish reds, notably Öküzgözü and Boğazkere, which produce deeply coloured, structured wines.

**Character** — Vineyards sit at high elevation under a harsh continental climate with hot summers and very cold winters. **Good to know** — its native grapes are prized for giving Turkish reds a distinctive identity unavailable anywhere else.

name: Galilee
description:
**Galilee** is the mountainous north of Israel and is widely regarded as the country's finest wine region, taking in the Upper Galilee and the elevated Golan Heights. Cool air and altitude make it stand out in a generally warm land.

**Wines & grapes** — Bordeaux varieties lead, especially Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah for reds, alongside whites such as Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.

**Character** — High elevation, cool nights and volcanic and limestone soils help the grapes ripen while keeping acidity and freshness. **Good to know** — many of Israel's most respected wineries source their top fruit from here.

name: Abava
description:
**Abava** takes its name from a river valley in Latvia and represents the northern, cold-climate fringe of European wine growing. Grape wine is a small and relatively recent pursuit in this Baltic country.

**Wines & grapes** — What is made comes mainly from cold-hardy hybrid grapes, and fruit and berry wines are also common in the region.

**Character** — The climate is cool and continental with a short growing season, so wines tend to be light and fresh, produced by small-scale growers working near the limits of viticulture.

name: Moselle Luxembourgeoise
description:
**Moselle Luxembourgeoise** is Luxembourg's stretch of the Moselle river valley, running along the country's eastern border, and is home to nearly all of its wine. It is a small but well-organised region with a strong white-wine and sparkling tradition.

**Wines & grapes** — Whites dominate, including Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois, Elbling and Rivaner (Müller-Thurgau), and the region is known for its crisp Crémant de Luxembourg sparkling wines.

**Character** — A cool northern climate and steep riverside slopes give wines that are light, fresh and high in acidity. **Good to know** — the wines share much of the character of neighbouring German and French Moselle vineyards.

name: Sonoma Coast
description:
**Sonoma Coast** is a cool-climate California wine region running along the Pacific in Sonoma County. It has become one of the United States' most respected addresses for elegant, restrained New World wines.

**Wines & grapes** — Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are the stars, joined by cool-climate Syrah, in styles that favour freshness and finesse over sheer power.

**Character** — Ocean fog and chilly breezes off the Pacific slow ripening, preserving bright acidity and delicate aromatics in the grapes. **Good to know** — the coolest, most fog-influenced sites are sometimes bottled under the tighter West Sonoma Coast designation.

name: Granada
description:
**Granada** is a province in Andalusia, in southern Spain, better known for its Moorish history than its wine, yet home to some of Europe's highest vineyards on the slopes below the Sierra Nevada. Its modern wine scene has grown around these mountain sites.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds, whites and rosés are made from a broad mix of Spanish and international varieties, with high-altitude planting a defining theme.

**Character** — Extreme elevation offsets the southern latitude, giving cool nights and a long ripening season that lend the wines surprising freshness for so warm a region.

name: Canary Islands, Tenerife
description:
**Canary Islands, Tenerife** is a volcanic island off the northwest coast of Africa, part of Spain, whose vineyards climb the flanks of the Teide volcano and rank among the most dramatic in Europe.

**Wines & grapes** — Both colours are made, largely from indigenous grapes rarely seen elsewhere: the red Listán Negro and the white Listán Blanco (the local name for Palomino), alongside aromatic Malvasía and other old varieties.

**Character** — Because the islands escaped the phylloxera louse, many vines grow ungrafted and are extremely old, some trained in low braided ropes across black volcanic ash. The wines often show a smoky, mineral, slightly saline streak that reflects the porous volcanic soils and the tug of the Atlantic.

**Good to know** — The high-altitude vineyards let growers keep freshness despite the subtropical latitude.

name: Moravia
description:
**Moravia** is the southeastern corner of the Czech Republic and the country's main winegrowing area, accounting for the great majority of Czech vineyards.

**Wines & grapes** — The focus is on crisp white wines from varieties familiar across central Europe, such as Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Müller-Thurgau and Riesling, with lighter reds also produced.

**Character** — This is a cool, continental climate on the northern edge of viable viticulture, which favours bright acidity and fresh, aromatic whites rather than heavy, high-alcohol styles. Much of the wine is enjoyed young and locally.

name: Thermenregion
description:
**Thermenregion** is a small Austrian wine region just south of Vienna, named for the warm thermal springs of the area.

**Wines & grapes** — It is best known for distinctive white wines from two local grapes, Zierfandler and Rotgipfler, which are often blended together; the region also grows red varieties including Sankt Laurent and Pinot Noir.

**Character** — The wines tend to be full-bodied and richly textured for Austrian whites, with ripe stone-fruit character balanced by firm acidity. The relatively warm, sheltered setting on the eastern slopes helps the fruit ripen fully.

name: Kent
description:
**Kent** is a county in southeast England, long nicknamed the Garden of England, and one of the heartlands of the country's fast-growing wine scene.

**Wines & grapes** — The specialty is traditional-method sparkling wine built from the Champagne trio of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier; aromatic still whites, notably from Bacchus, are also made.

**Character** — Kent's vineyards sit on chalk and greensand, the chalk belonging to the same seam that dips beneath the Channel and resurfaces in Champagne, and its cool, marginal climate preserves the high acidity that gives English sparkling wine its taut, refreshing edge.

**Good to know** — Warmer recent vintages have made ripening far more reliable than a generation ago.

name: Gelderland
description:
**Gelderland** is a province in the eastern Netherlands where a small number of vineyards have appeared as Dutch winemaking has slowly expanded.

**Wines & grapes** — Production is modest and leans on cool-climate and disease-resistant hybrid varieties suited to a northern setting, making mostly white and some red and sparkling wines.

**Character** — This is a cool, marginal growing climate, so the wines are typically light and fresh with lively acidity, made in small volumes and enjoyed largely within the region.

name: Hardanger
description:
**Hardanger** is a fjord district in western Norway, one of the northernmost places in the world where fruit is cultivated for drinks.

**Wines & grapes** — The area is far better known for its orchards and traditional ciders than for grape wine, and any grape production is tiny and experimental in this extreme climate.

**Character** — Long summer daylight and the moderating effect of the fjord allow fruit to ripen despite the high latitude, giving crisp, aromatic and high-acid drinks. Expect small-scale, artisanal bottlings.

name: Sonoma Valley
description:
**Sonoma Valley** is a classic winegrowing valley in Sonoma County, north of San Francisco, and one of California's most historic wine districts.

**Wines & grapes** — It produces a broad range: powerful Cabernet Sauvignon and old-vine Zinfandel from warmer sites, plus Chardonnay and Pinot Noir where cooling coastal air reaches in.

**Character** — The valley is shaped by fog and breezes drawn up from San Pablo Bay, which stretch the ripening season and add freshness to the ripe, generous fruit. Soils and elevation vary widely between the valley floor and the surrounding hills.

**Good to know** — Sonoma is often seen as a more laid-back, farm-rooted counterpart to neighbouring Napa.

name: Occitanie
description:
**Occitanie** is a large administrative region sweeping across the south of France from the Mediterranean toward the Atlantic, taking in the historic Languedoc-Roussillon vineyards and part of the southwest.

**Wines & grapes** — As one of the biggest wine-producing zones in the world, it makes every style: robust reds from Grenache, Syrah, Carignan and Mourvèdre, fresh whites and rosés, plus sparkling and fortified wines.

**Character** — The sunny, dry Mediterranean climate ripens fruit easily, yielding warm, generous, herb-scented wines, while cooler hillsides and Atlantic-influenced pockets add variety.

**Good to know** — The region spans everything from great-value everyday bottles to ambitious estate wines.

name: Zürich
description:
**Zürich** is a canton in German-speaking Switzerland where vineyards cluster around the lake and river valleys near the city of the same name.

**Wines & grapes** — The mainstay red is Pinot Noir, known locally as Blauburgunder, while the leading white is Müller-Thurgau, often called Riesling-Silvaner in Switzerland.

**Character** — This is a cool, northerly climate, so the reds tend to be light and fragrant and the whites crisp and delicate. Production is small and rarely leaves the country, meaning most of these wines are enjoyed close to where they are grown.

name: North Otago
description:
**North Otago** sits on the eastern side of New Zealand's South Island, just north of the better-known Central Otago, and centres on the emerging Waitaki Valley.

**Wines & grapes** — The focus is on cool-climate varieties, especially elegant Pinot Noir along with aromatic whites such as Riesling and Pinot Gris.

**Character** — What sets the area apart is its limestone-rich soils, unusual in New Zealand, which growers believe lend the wines a fine, mineral, tautly structured quality. The cool, sometimes frost-prone climate keeps acidity bright and the wines restrained rather than showy.

name: Mount Benson
description:
**Mount Benson** is a small, coastal wine region on the Limestone Coast of South Australia, facing the Southern Ocean.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds lead the way, particularly Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon, with some white varieties also grown.

**Character** — Its position right by the sea gives a maritime, wind-swept climate that is more moderate than inland South Australia, producing reds that tend to be medium-bodied with fresh acidity and a savoury edge. The limestone-influenced soils give the wider coast its name.

name: Paarl
description:
**Paarl** is a warm inland district in South Africa's Western Cape, set around a large granite outcrop north of Stellenbosch and long a hub of the country's wine industry.

**Wines & grapes** — It makes a wide spread of styles: full reds from Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Rhône varieties, versatile Chenin Blanc, and other whites, plus some fortified wines.

**Character** — The climate is notably warmer than the coastal districts, so the wines are typically ripe, generous and full-bodied, though cooler, higher slopes add freshness. Soils range from granite to shale across the valley.

**Good to know** — Paarl was historically the home of the KWV, the giant cooperative that once shaped South African wine.

name: Hokkaido
description:
**Hokkaido** is Japan's northernmost main island and one of the country's most promising cool-climate wine frontiers, with vineyards clustered around towns like Yoichi and across the Sorachi area.

**Wines & grapes** — Aromatic, crisp whites lead the way, made from cold-hardy varieties such as Kerner, Müller-Thurgau and Bacchus, alongside lighter reds and rosés from Zweigelt and Pinot Noir. A handful of growers also work with local and hybrid grapes suited to the cold.

**Character** — Long, snowy winters and a short but bright growing season give the wines fresh acidity and restraint. The maritime setting and northern latitude make this a place for delicate, high-toned styles rather than big, ripe ones — and interest in it has grown quickly as Japanese wine has matured.

name: Lake Erie
description:
**Lake Erie** is a grape-growing belt along the southern shore of the Great Lake of the same name in the United States, a broad zone that has long been one of the largest vineyard areas in the eastern part of the country.

**Wines & grapes** — Historically the region was dominated by Concord and other native American (labrusca) grapes grown for juice and jelly, but it now also produces wine from Riesling, Chardonnay, hybrids and other vinifera varieties.

**Character** — The huge body of water acts as a heat buffer, softening winter cold and delaying spring frost, which lets vines survive and ripen where they otherwise might struggle. Wines range from sweet, grapey styles to crisp, cool-climate whites.

name: Maldonado
description:
**Maldonado** is a coastal department in southeastern Uruguay, facing the Atlantic near the resort of Punta del Este, and one of the country's more exciting newer areas for quality wine.

**Wines & grapes** — Tannat, Uruguay's signature red, is grown here, but the district is especially associated with fresher, coastal styles including Albariño and other whites, plus lighter reds.

**Character** — Ocean breezes and cooler maritime conditions set it apart from Uruguay's more established inland vineyards, encouraging wines with bright acidity and a saline, refreshing edge. It remains a small, ambitious region still building its reputation.

name: Vale do Sao Francisco
description:
**Vale do Sao Francisco** is a wine region in the arid northeast of Brazil, spread along the São Francisco River not far from the equator — one of the few places on earth making wine in a genuinely tropical setting.

**Wines & grapes** — Reds from Syrah lead here, with other international varieties grown for both still and sparkling wines.

**Character** — The extraordinary feature is the climate: hot, dry and irrigated, with enough year-round warmth that vines never fully rest, allowing growers to prune for more than one harvest per year. The wines are warm and fruit-forward, and the region is a fascinating example of viticulture pushed to the tropics.

name: Istria
description:
**Istria** is a peninsula reaching into the Adriatic Sea in northwestern Croatia, a green, hilly area as famous for its olive oil and truffles as for its wine.

**Wines & grapes** — The flagship white is Malvazija Istarska (Istrian Malvasia), which ranges from fresh and floral to richer, skin-contact and barrel-aged styles. The main red is Teran, a deeply coloured, tangy grape, alongside plantings of international varieties.

**Character** — A Mediterranean climate tempered by the sea, combined with distinctive red and white soils, gives the wines vibrant acidity and a savoury, mineral quality. Istria has become one of the most respected wine areas of the eastern Adriatic.

name: Central Ranges
description:
**Central Ranges** is a wine zone in New South Wales, Australia, sitting inland on the higher country west of the Blue Mountains and taking in districts such as Mudgee, Orange and Cowra.

**Wines & grapes** — A wide spread of varieties is grown across its sub-regions, including Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, with cooler, higher sites favouring more elegant styles.

**Character** — Altitude is the defining thread here: many vineyards sit well above the surrounding plains, which brings cooler nights and helps the grapes keep freshness. That variation in elevation gives the zone real diversity, from ripe, generous reds to bright, restrained whites.

name: Geelong
description:
